title: Why should you first clarify what "1 million users" means (registered vs daily-active vs concurrent) before designing, since the real driver is requests/sec, read/write ratio, data size, and latency/consistency requirements?
shortTitle: Why should you first clarify what "1 million users" means

s1_definition.profdef: Before designing for scale, you must translate a vague headline number like "one million users" into the concrete engineering drivers that actually size a system: requests per second, the read-to-write ratio, total and growth data size, and the latency and consistency requirements. "One million users" is ambiguous because it could mean registered users (most of whom are inactive), daily-active users, or concurrent users at peak, and these differ by orders of magnitude. The right design depends entirely on which one and on the derived load, so clarifying the number first prevents either massive over-engineering or a system that collapses under real peak traffic.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine someone tells the National Bank of India "we have a million customers, build a branch big enough." That sentence alone tells you almost nothing about how many counters to build. A million customers on the books might mean only fifty thousand visit in a day, and of those maybe two thousand are inside the branch at the busiest moment on salary day. If you built counters for a million people standing at once, you would waste a fortune on an empty hall. If you built for the average day but ignored the salary-day rush, the branch would overflow and customers would be turned away. So before pouring any concrete, a good architect asks: how many are actually inside at peak, how many just read their balance versus make a transaction, how much paperwork do we store, and how fast must each customer be served? Those answers, not the headline count, decide the design.
s1_definition.oneliner: "One million users" is a marketing number, not an engineering one — you must convert it into peak requests per second, read-to-write ratio, data size, and latency and consistency targets before you can design anything.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Before designing for scale, you must translate a vague headline number like "one million users" into the concrete engineering drivers that actually size a system: requests per second, the read-to-write ratio, total and growth data size, and the latency and consistency requirements. "One million users" is ambiguous because it could mean registered users (most of whom are inactive), daily-active users, or concurrent users at peak, and these differ by orders of magnitude. The right design depends entirely on which one and on the derived load, so clarifying the number first prevents either massive over-engineering or a system that collapses under real peak traffic.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine someone tells the National Bank of India "we have a million customers, build a branch big enough." That sentence alone tells you almost nothing about how many counters to build. A million customers on the books might mean only fifty thousand visit in a day, and of those maybe two thousand are inside the branch at the busiest moment on salary day. If you built counters for a million people standing at once, you would waste a fortune on an empty hall. If you built for the average day but ignored the salary-day rush, the branch would overflow and customers would be turned away. So before pouring any concrete, a good architect asks: how many are actually inside at peak, how many just read their balance versus make a transaction, how much paperwork do we store, and how fast must each customer be served? Those answers, not the headline count, decide the design.

**One line to remember:** "One million users" is a marketing number, not an engineering one — you must convert it into peak requests per second, read-to-write ratio, data size, and latency and consistency targets before you can design anything.

sections.s2_technical:
The core issue is ambiguity. Registered users are everyone who ever signed up, and most are dormant. Daily-active users are those who actually use the system in a day. Concurrent users are those active at the same instant, and peak concurrency is what hardware must survive. These three can differ by one or two orders of magnitude: a million registered users might translate to a hundred thousand daily-active and only a few thousand concurrent at peak. Designing for the wrong one of these is the classic mistake that leads either to wasteful over-provisioning or to an outage on the first busy day.

The real engineering driver is requests per second, especially peak requests per second, not users. You derive it. If a hundred thousand daily-active users each make, say, thirty requests spread over the active hours, that is a few million requests per day, which averages to a modest rate, but traffic is never flat. You apply a peak-to-average multiplier, often three to ten times, to account for salary day, market open, or a marketing push. The peak number is what you size load balancers, instance counts, and connection pools against, because a system sized for the average falls over at the peak.

The read-to-write ratio shapes the entire data strategy. A read-heavy system, like checking balances, benefits enormously from caching and read replicas, because you can serve most traffic without touching the primary database. A write-heavy system, like recording transactions, benefits from write batching, asynchronous processing, sharding, and careful primary-database tuning, because writes cannot simply be cached away. Knowing the ratio tells you where to spend your scaling effort, so a ninety-to-ten read-heavy workload and a fifty-fifty workload lead to very different architectures.

Data size and its growth rate drive storage and partitioning decisions. Ten gigabytes fits comfortably on one node, while ten terabytes growing by a terabyte a month forces you to think about sharding, archival, and tiered storage early. You estimate rows per entity, bytes per row, and growth per month, because the data volume decides whether a single database suffices or whether you must partition from the start.

Latency and consistency requirements are the final, often decisive, drivers. A tight latency target, like a p99 under a hundred milliseconds, forces caching, co-location, and possibly multi-region edges. Consistency requirements are even more fundamental: a bank balance that must be strictly correct demands strong consistency and transactional guarantees, which constrain how aggressively you can cache, replicate, and distribute, whereas a social feed can tolerate eventual consistency and scale much more freely. The senior-level point is that these requirements can pull in opposite directions, and only by knowing them precisely can you make the right trade-offs. The whole exercise of clarifying the number is really about deriving these four drivers, because they, not the headline user count, determine capacity, data architecture, and the consistency model.
sections.s3_banking:
A product manager at the National Bank of India told the engineering team "we are launching to one million users, make sure it scales." The team almost over-built a massive distributed system before an architect insisted on clarifying the number.

Problem 1 — "one million users" was taken literally as a million concurrent, so the first capacity estimate was wildly oversized and would have wasted enormous infrastructure spend. This is exactly why you must distinguish registered, daily-active, and concurrent users: the real concurrent peak was a tiny fraction of the registered count.

Problem 2 — the initial sizing assumed flat average traffic, which would have collapsed on salary day when everyone checks balances and transfers at once. This is exactly why you apply a peak-to-average multiplier to derive peak requests per second.

Problem 3 — the team planned to cache everything aggressively, including balances, until they realized balances require strong consistency and the workload was heavily read-skewed for balance checks but write-critical for transfers. This is exactly why the read-to-write ratio and consistency requirements must be known before choosing a caching and consistency strategy.

The mini-project builds a `UserProfile` capturing registered, daily-active, and concurrent counts, a `LoadEstimator` that derives peak requests per second, read-to-write split, data size, and whether strong consistency is required, and a `CapacityPlan` that reports the derived drivers. The demo takes the headline "one million users," clarifies it into realistic active and concurrent figures, and prints the true engineering drivers that should size the design.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the headline figure of one million users, plus realistic assumptions that ten percent are daily-active, three percent of those are concurrent at peak, each active user makes thirty requests a day, traffic peaks at eight times the average, the workload is ninety percent reads, balances need strong consistency, and the latency target is a hundred milliseconds at the ninety-ninth percentile.

Step 1: The naive reading treats one million as concurrent, which would size the system for a million simultaneous requests and lead to a massive over-build. The demo flags this as the mistake to avoid.

Step 2: The number is clarified. One million registered becomes one hundred thousand daily-active at ten percent, and three thousand concurrent at peak at three percent of daily-active. These three figures differ by orders of magnitude, which is the whole point.

Step 3: Average requests per second is derived from the daily-active users, not the registered count. One hundred thousand active users times thirty requests is three million requests a day, which over eighty-six thousand four hundred seconds is roughly thirty-five requests per second on average.

Step 4: Peak requests per second is derived by applying the eight-times multiplier, giving roughly two hundred eighty requests per second at peak. This peak figure, far smaller than a million but larger than the flat average, is what the hardware must actually survive.

Step 5: The peak is split by the read-to-write ratio: ninety percent reads and ten percent writes, so about two hundred fifty read requests and twenty-eight write requests per second at peak. This tells the team to invest in caching and read replicas for the reads while tuning the primary for the smaller write load.

Step 6: Data growth is derived from transactions per active user per year and bytes per row, giving a storage growth figure, and the strong-consistency and latency requirements are recorded. The conclusion is explicit: size the system for a few hundred peak requests per second with strong consistency on balances and a tight latency target, not for a million concurrent users.

```
2026-10-24 12:45:00 SEVERE  NAIVE: treating 1,000,000 as CONCURRENT -> massive over-build
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    CLARIFY: registered=1000000 dailyActive=100000 concurrentPeak=3000
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    DERIVED peakRps=277 (read 249/write 27), data/yr=67GB
2026-10-24 12:45:00 WARNING CONSISTENCY: strong required (balances) -> limit aggressive caching of balances
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    === Engineering drivers that actually size the system ===
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    Average rps: 34
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    Peak rps: 277 (reads 249, writes 27)
2026-10-24 12:45:00 INFO    CONCLUSION: size for ~277 peak rps, NOT for 1,000,000 concurrent.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Before I design anything for scale, I insist on clarifying what a number like one million users actually means, because on its own it is a marketing figure, not an engineering one. The word users is ambiguous across three very different things: registered users, which is everyone who ever signed up and is mostly dormant; daily-active users, who actually use the system in a day; and concurrent users, who are active at the same instant, with peak concurrency being what the hardware must survive. These can differ by one or two orders of magnitude, so a million registered users might be only a hundred thousand daily-active and a few thousand concurrent at peak. Designing for the wrong one is the classic mistake that leads either to a wildly expensive over-build or to an outage on the first busy day.

What I really want are four derived drivers. The first is peak requests per second, not users. I derive average requests per second from the daily-active count and a per-user request rate, then I apply a peak-to-average multiplier, often three to ten times, to account for bursts like salary day or market open, because a system sized for the average collapses at the peak. The second is the read-to-write ratio, which shapes the whole data strategy: a read-heavy balance-checking workload benefits enormously from caching and read replicas, while a write-heavy transaction workload needs batching, async processing, sharding, and primary-database tuning, because writes cannot simply be cached away.

The third driver is data size and its growth rate, which decides whether a single database suffices or whether I must shard and archive from the start, and I estimate it from rows per entity, bytes per row, and growth per month. The fourth, and often the decisive one, is latency and consistency requirements. A tight latency target forces caching, co-location, and sometimes multi-region edges, and consistency is even more fundamental: a bank balance that must be exactly correct demands strong consistency and transactional guarantees, which limit how aggressively I can cache and distribute, whereas something like a social feed tolerates eventual consistency and scales far more freely.

I lived this on a banking launch where a product manager said build for one million users, and the first instinct was to treat that as a million concurrent and over-build a huge distributed system. Once we clarified it into about a hundred thousand daily-active and a few thousand concurrent at peak, and derived a peak of only a few hundred requests per second with strong consistency on balances and a tight latency target, the right-sized design was dramatically simpler and cheaper, yet still safe for salary-day peaks.

The way I summarize it for an interviewer is that one million users is the start of the conversation, not the answer. The real work is converting that headline into peak requests per second, the read-to-write ratio, data size and growth, and the latency and consistency requirements, because those four drivers, not the user count, determine capacity, data architecture, and the consistency model. Clarify first, derive the drivers, and only then design.
